errors: None found. I checked every entry for a = 1 to 58 by direct multiplication, e.g. 30²+1 = 901 = 17·53, 47²+1 = 2210 = 2·5·13·17, 55²+1 = 3026 = 2·17·89, 57²+1 = 3250 = 2·5³·13. I also confirmed that 1297, 1601, 2917 and 3137 are prime by testing the primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) up to their square roots.

ideas.what: Factor table of a²+1 used as a sieve to locate primes of the form a²+1 and of related forms (a²+1)/2, (a²+1)/5, (a²+1)/10.
ideas.modern_name: Sieve for primes in polynomial sequences (Landau's 4th problem; quadratic sieve idea of periodic divisibility mod p)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (tables of primes of the form a²+1); Landau's problem later; Chebyshev and Cunningham for later tables
ideas.where_published: E283 itself (Novi Commentarii 9, 1762/3, publ. 1764); related remarks in Euler's correspondence with Goldbach

ideas.what: Implicit fact that all odd prime divisors of a²+1 are ≡ 1 (mod 4) and recur periodically in a with period p (two residue classes).
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic residue character of −1; Fermat–Euler theorem on divisors of sums of two squares
ideas.where_published: E228, E241 (divisors of sums of two squares)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a correct, routine factor table supporting Euler's well-known prime-search method in E283. Nothing on the page is unpublished or unexpected.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image. Entry 47 should read 2.5.13.17 and entry 55 should read 2.17.89; the dots are missing only in the print. The trailing '59' is a catchword for the next page, not a table entry.
